$comment: YES / NO in Hinglish — the detector 236 authored pack items depend on and nothing provided.
WHY IT EXISTS. Every `answer_type: "boolean"` item in the question-pack corpus carries ZERO
options: measured, 236 of 236. So there is no chip to tap and no label to match, and the only
thing that arrives is a spoken or typed sentence. Without this file `normalizeFor` fell through
to the verbatim path and stored 'haan bilkul karta hoon' as the value of a BOOLEAN field.
NEGATIVES ARE NOT LISTED HERE. They are `negation.json`'s `negators` + `tagOnlyNegators`, read
through the negation engine. A second copy of 'nahi' is a second thing to keep in step, and the
negation engine already knows about clause splitting and the look-back window that decides
whether a negator reaches a given word.
TWO TIERS, AND THE ORDER MATTERS.
explicitCues  an unambiguous yes. 'haan', 'ji', 'bilkul', 'yes'. These are the answer.
verbCues      a first-person claim that IMPLIES yes — 'karta hoon', 'aata hai', 'kar leta
hoon'. A worker asked 'Kya aap gas charging karte hain?' very often answers
'karta hoon' with no 'haan' anywhere.
The verb tier is deliberately SECOND and deliberately narrow. It is the tier that can be wrong:
a worker who answers a gas-charging question with 'main welding karta hoon' is claiming a
different skill, and this file cannot tell. That is tolerable because the caller only ever
applies it to the question ON SCREEN — the one the worker was just asked — and because the
alternative it replaces was storing the whole sentence in a boolean column.
WHAT IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT. No hedges ('kabhi kabhi', 'thoda', 'shayad'). A boolean question
answered with 'sometimes' is genuinely ambiguous, and no cue matching it means the parser
returns null — the question stays askable and is then recorded as unanswered. Guessing there
would put a value a worker did not give into a matchable column.
ALSO ABSENT: bare 'ha' and bare 'hai'. 'hai' is the copula ('is') and appears in almost every
Hindi sentence; 'ha' is one edit from it. Either would fire on sentences that are not answers.
REGEX SUBSET: explicit character classes only, `{WB}`/`{WE}` for boundaries — never `\b`, `\d`
or `\w`. See README.md. The Devanagari alternatives are bracketed with `{DB}`/`{DE}` because a
word boundary does not work after a matra.
$comment_explicitCues: The optional trailing 'hai|hain|h' absorbs 'haan hai' / 'bilkul hai' without letting 'hai'
match on its own — it is a suffix of a listed cue, never an alternative to one.
'ji' has its own roman entry because it is the shortest cue in the list and the most likely to
be a whole utterance ('Ji.'). It carries an optional honorific so 'ji sir' does not need a
second pattern. It is NOT folded into the big alternation only because that alternation's
optional 'hai' suffix would make 'ji hai' match, which is not how anyone speaks.
ORDER INSIDE THE DEVANAGARI ALTERNATION IS LOAD-BEARING: the two-word 'जी हाँ' forms come
first, then the compounds, then bare 'जी'. A regex alternation takes the first branch that
matches, so putting 'जी' earlier would make it win on 'जी हाँ' and report a one-character span
where a two-word cue stands. No pattern here may be optional as a whole — an alternation that
can match the empty string matches at every offset and would report a cue in any text at all.
$comment_standaloneNegatives: Whole-utterance negatives that `negation.json` deliberately does NOT carry, and the reason the
split is real rather than a loophole.
`negation.json`'s negators are SCOPING operators — the engine blanks the words they deny.
English 'no' is not one of those; it is an answer token. Putting it in the shared list would
make 'no. 5 gali' blank '5', in every detector, in both languages. Here it reaches nothing but
Matched as whole trimmed TOKENS, not as regexes, so 'no' cannot fire inside 'note' or 'nozzle'.
$comment_verbCues: 'ki' in the fifth pattern is risky on its own — it is also the Hindi genitive particle ('X ki
Y'). It is kept because the trailing 'hai|hain|hoon|tha|thi' group is what disambiguates in
practice ('kiya hai' vs 'gaadi ki chabi'), and because this tier is only consulted when no
explicit yes/no cue was found at all. If it measures badly in the field, delete this one
